job.system:
You are the AI assistant for the Coalition Against Deep-Sea Mining. Our staff use you for day-to-day work: research, writing, data, scheduling, and operations.

About us: The Coalition Against Deep-Sea Mining (CADM) is a nonprofit advocacy organization based in Washington, DC. We believe that the industrial mining of the deep seabed, meaning the large-scale extraction of minerals from the ocean floor, poses a serious risk of irreversible destruction to deep-ocean ecosystems, and that no one currently knows how to conduct it without such damage. Our goal is a legally binding prohibition on commercial deep-sea mining, first in the United States and then through an international treaty. We work through lobbying, grassroots organizing, and public education.

Current focus: Our top priority this fall is S. 2817, the Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act, which we strongly support. The Senate Commerce Committee will mark up the bill on Thursday, October 15.

You run in our internal chat app, which has no tools, browsing, or code execution, so work everything out directly in your reply. Staff rely on your work, so be accurate and thorough.
job.prompt:
Before next Thursday's markup, can you go through the bill text below and find every loophole, ambiguity, or drafting problem: anything that would let companies keep going, or that would make the bill hard to enforce or easy to challenge?

Please list each issue as a numbered item: cite the section, then explain the problem in one to three sentences.

---

S. 2817 — Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act
(text as amended by the manager's amendment of October 6, 2026)

SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE.
This Act may be cited as the "Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act".

SEC. 2. DEFINITIONS.
In this Act:
(1) COMMERCIAL DEEP SEABED MINING.—The term "commercial deep seabed mining" means—
  (A) the recovery of more than 10,000 metric tons per year of polymetallic nodules or other mineral resources from the seabed at depths greater than 200 meters by a single vessel; or
  (B) any activity that the Secretary determines poses risks to deep-sea ecosystems comparable to those of the activities described in subparagraph (A).
(2) U.S. PERSON.—The term "U.S. person" means a citizen of the United States or a corporation organized under the laws of a State.
(3) COVERED VESSEL.—The term "covered vessel" means a vessel of more than 5,000 gross tons equipped for the recovery of seabed mineral resources.

SEC. 3. PROHIBITION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—It shall be unlawful for any person in the United States, or any U.S. person anywhere, to engage in commercial deep seabed mining.
(b) EXISTING OPERATIONS.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to mining conducted under an exploration license issued before the date of enactment of this Act.
(c) ENVIRONMENTAL ASSESSMENT.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to activities conducted for the purpose of environmental assessment.

SEC. 4. REGISTRY.
(a) REGISTRATION.—The operator of each covered vessel shall register the vessel with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.
(b) REPORTS.—Each registered operator shall submit to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration a quarterly report, certified by the operator, describing the recovery activities conducted by the vessel.

SEC. 5. PENALTIES.
(a) CIVIL PENALTY.—Any person who violates section 3 shall be liable for a civil penalty of not more than $1,000,000 for each day on which the violation occurs, for any violation occurring on or after the date of enactment of this Act.
(b) CRIMINAL PENALTY.—Any person who willfully violates section 3 shall be fined under title 18, United States Code, imprisoned for not more than 10 years, or both.

SEC. 6. INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT.
The Secretary of State shall seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months after the date of enactment of this Act, an international agreement establishing prohibitions equivalent to those in section 3.

SEC. 7. DURATION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—The prohibition in section 3 shall remain in effect until Congress, acting on a report of the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, finds by joint resolution that commercial deep seabed mining can be conducted without serious harm.
(b) SUNSET.—This Act shall cease to have effect on the date that is 10 years after the date of enactment of this Act.

SEC. 8. EFFECTIVE DATE.
This Act shall take effect 180 days after the date of enactment.

---

result:
# S. 2817 Issue List (Manager's Amendment of Oct. 6)

## Sec. 2: Definitions

1. **§2(1)(A), per-vessel threshold.** The 10,000-ton limit applies "by a single vessel," so an operator can split recovery across several vessels, each under 10,000 tons, with no aggregation rule. The limit should apply per operator, including affiliates, or be removed.

2. **§2(1)(A), threshold level.** At 10,000 tons per vessel per year, pilot and "collector test" operations remain lawful. That lets companies build the technical record and investor case for commercial mining. Industry pilot tests have recovered a few thousand tons.

3. **§2(1)(A), "by a single vessel."** Recovery by a fixed platform, a riser or pipeline to an installation, or seabed-based equipment isn't "by a vessel" and falls outside the definition entirely. When one vessel runs the collector and another lifts or carries the ore, it's unclear which vessel "recovers" it.

4. **§2(1)(A), "from the seabed."** "Seabed" isn't defined, so it's unclear whether drilling or cutting into the subsoil is covered, such as seafloor massive sulfides or crust removal. "Mineral resources" also isn't defined. If read broadly, it could sweep in deepwater oil, gas, or sand and gravel, which invites industry opposition and challenges.

5. **§2(1)(A), "per year."** The bill doesn't say whether this means a calendar year, a fiscal year, or a rolling 12 months. It also doesn't say how tonnage is measured: wet or dry weight, ore or concentrate, landed or lifted.

6. **§2(1)(B), "the Secretary."** "Secretary" is never defined anywhere in the Act, so no agency clearly holds this authority.

7. **§2(1)(B), open-ended delegation.** The Secretary can designate new prohibited activities with no procedure (no notice-and-comment requirement) and only a vague standard ("comparable" risks). Because §5(b) attaches criminal penalties, this invites vagueness, due process, and nondelegation challenges. It also has no effect if a hostile Secretary simply never acts.

8. **§2(2), "U.S. person" excludes LLCs and partnerships.** Only "a corporation organized under the laws of a State" is covered. LLCs, partnerships, trusts, and other entities, which are common vehicles for mining ventures, aren't U.S. persons, and this is probably the biggest loophole in the bill.

9. **§2(2), foreign subsidiaries and parents.** A U.S. company can operate abroad through a foreign-incorporated subsidiary, and foreign-incorporated firms with U.S. operations or ownership aren't covered outside U.S. territory. Lawful permanent residents are also excluded.

10. **§2(2), "State" undefined.** The bill doesn't say whether "State" includes D.C., Puerto Rico, or other territories. Corporations organized there may fall outside the definition.

11. **§2(3), "covered vessel."** This term is used only in §4, not in the prohibition. The 5,000-gross-ton floor means smaller vessels, the same ones that can stay under the §2(1)(A) cap, never register. "Equipped for recovery" is also undefined: it's unclear whether a vessel that can be refitted counts.

## Sec. 3: Prohibition

12. **§3(a), "in the United States" undefined.** The bill doesn't say whether this covers the territorial sea, the EEZ, the outer continental shelf, or the territories. A foreign company mining in the U.S. EEZ could argue it isn't "in the United States."

13. **§3(a), narrow conduct.** Only "engag[ing] in" mining is barred. Financing, chartering or supplying vessels, sponsoring, insuring, buying, importing, or processing deep-sea-mined minerals are all untouched. U.S. capital and markets can keep supporting foreign operations.

14. **§3(a), no flag-state hook.** A U.S.-flagged vessel run by a foreign operator isn't clearly covered, and the bill doesn't bar foreign-flagged vessels operated from U.S. ports.

15. **§3(a), government entities.** "Person" likely excludes federal agencies under the Dictionary Act. That leaves open government-sponsored mining, for example for defense stockpiles.

16. **§3(b), "exploration license" exemption.** The exemption covers "mining," not just exploration, under any pre-enactment exploration license. A license holder could conduct full commercial recovery with no time limit.

17. **§3(b), issuer and transfers.** The bill doesn't say who must have issued the license. It could include DSHMRA licenses, ISA exploration contracts, or foreign-state licenses. It's also silent on renewals, extensions, modifications, and transfers, so grandfathered rights could be sold or extended indefinitely.

18. **§3(b), rush to license.** Pegging the cutoff to enactment, not introduction, rewards rushing applications while the bill is pending.

19. **§3(c), "environmental assessment."** The exemption has no definition, no scale or tonnage limit, no permit or oversight requirement, and no ban on selling recovered material. A company could label pilot or commercial mining as "assessment."

20. **§3, DSHMRA conflict.** The bill doesn't amend or repeal the Deep Seabed Hard Mineral Resources Act (30 U.S.C. 1401 et seq.). That leaves NOAA's authority to issue commercial recovery permits nominally intact and sets up conflicts over pending and future permits. It should expressly bar issuing permits and revoke or freeze pending applications.

## Sec. 4: Registry

21. **§4, no penalties.** §5 penalizes only violations of §3. Failing to register, failing to report, or filing false reports carries no penalty under this Act; 18 U.S.C. §1001 might apply, but the bill doesn't say so.

22. **§4, no deadlines or content.** There's no deadline to register, no required report content (tonnage, location, depth, buyers), and no rule on whether reports are public.

23. **§4, no verification.** Reports are self-certified, with no inspection, observer, vessel-tracking, or records-access authority for NOAA.

24. **§4, no jurisdictional nexus.** The registry applies to "each covered vessel" worldwide, with no U.S. connection. That invites extraterritoriality challenges and makes it unenforceable against foreign vessels.

## Sec. 5: Penalties

25. **§5(a) vs. §8, conflicting dates.** Civil penalties apply to violations "on or after the date of enactment," but the Act takes effect 180 days later. That creates an internal contradiction and a retroactivity argument for anyone penalized during the gap.

26. **§5(a), "each day" vs. an annual threshold.** A violation is defined by annual tonnage, so it's unclear on which "day" a violation occurs. It could be only the day the cap is exceeded, or every day of operation, which makes calculating penalties hard to defend.

27. **§5, no enforcement machinery.** The bill names no enforcing agency. It doesn't say whether civil penalties are assessed administratively or in court, and it has no hearing procedure, investigative or boarding authority, venue or jurisdiction provision, or Coast Guard role.

28. **§5, no forfeiture or injunctions.** There's no forfeiture of vessels, equipment, or recovered minerals, no injunctive relief, and no citizen suit. A daily fine capped "not more than" $1M, with no minimum, may simply be a cost of doing business for a large operation.

## Sec. 6: International Agreement

29. **§6, ambiguous and hortatory.** "Shall seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months" doesn't say whether the deadline applies to starting negotiations or concluding them. Either way, there's no obligation of result and no reporting requirement. "Equivalent to those in section 3" would also export every loophole above.

## Sec. 7: Duration

30. **§7(a) vs. §7(b), conflicting durations.** Subsection (a) says the ban lasts until Congress finds mining safe, while (b) ends the entire Act after 10 years regardless. The hard sunset lets industry wait it out, and it ends the registry and penalties too.

31. **§7(a), weak lifting mechanism.** The bill doesn't require anyone to commission the National Academies report, and "serious harm" is undefined. A future Congress could pass a joint resolution citing any report.

## Sec. 8 and Overall Structure

32. **§8, 180-day delay.** Mining is lawful for six months after enactment. That window allows a rush of operations and the stockpiling of recovered nodules.

33. **Whole bill, no severability clause.** If a court strikes down §2(1)(B) or an extraterritorial application, opponents can argue the whole Act falls.

34. **Whole bill, no rulemaking authority.** No agency is given authority to issue regulations implementing the prohibition, the registry, or the definitions.

**Highest-priority fixes for the markup:**
- The LLC gap (#8)
- The per-vessel threshold and aggregation (#1–3)
- The exploration-license exemption (#16–17)
- The environmental-assessment exemption (#19)
- The undefined "United States" (#12)
- The 10-year sunset (#30)

This review is based only on the text you provided. Counsel should check items like #15 and #20 against current law and any pending DSHMRA applications before you circulate amendment language.
